ety.text: From Middle English sonn, sone, sun, sune, from Old English sunu (“son”), from Proto-West Germanic *sunu, from Proto-Germanic *sunuz (“son”), from Proto-Indo-European *suHnús (“son”), from Proto-Indo-European *sewH- (“to bear; give birth”).
From Middle English sonen, sunen, from the noun (see above).
From Spanish son (literally “tone, sound”).

senses.d: One's male offspring.
ex: Before the birth of the man's child, he said: "I want a son, not a daughter."
From what conſummate vertue I have choſe / This perfect Man, by merit call'd my Son,

senses.d: A male adopted person in relation to his adoptive parents.
A male person who has such a close relationship with an older or otherwise more authoritative person that he can be regarded as a son of the other person.
ex: Eli called Samuel his son. Be plain, good son, and homely in thy drift.

senses.d: A male person considered to have been significantly shaped by social conflict.
ex: He was a son of the mafia system.

senses.d: A person regarded as the product of some place.
ex: I hold it to be true, that the people are the sons of the soil; and we are only their instruments here.

senses.d: A familiar address to a male person from an older or otherwise more authoritative person.
ex: Son, can't you see that she's just a little girl?

senses.d: An informal address to a friend or person of equal authority.
The current version of a file, derived from the preceding father file.
ex: Three generations of file are usually kept, being the grandfather, father and son files.

senses.d: To produce (i.e. bear, father, beget) a son.
ex: I sonned a father who would not be sonned, […]

senses.d: To address (someone) as "son".
ex: “Don't 'son' me.” “I'm old enough to be your father,” he said with a dismissive wave of his hand.

senses.d: Son cubano, a genre of music and dance blending Spanish and African elements that originated in Cuba during the late 19th century.

grp.label: a male person in relation to his parents

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish fijo, from Latin fīlius.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese filho (“son”), from Latin fīlius (“son”), from Old Latin fīlios (“son”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Compare Galician fillo, Spanish hijo and Sicilian figghiu.

Inherited from Old French fils, fiz, fil, from Latin filius (“son”). Cognate to Spanish hijo, Portuguese filho, , Italian figlio and Romanian fiu, among others. Final -s regularly became mute before consonants in late Old French but was then still pronounced in pausa.

From Latin fīlius, from Old Latin fīlios, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Cognate to French fils, Portuguese filho, Galician fillo, Romanian fiu, Spanish hijo, Sicilian figghiu, Corsican figliu, Sardinian fillu, Romansh fegl.
From Latin fīliolus. By surface analysis, figlio (“son”) + -olo (diminutive suffix).

phr: I'll be a son of a gun

ety.text: From Middle English song, sang, from Old English sang, from Proto-West Germanic *sangu, from Proto-Germanic *sangwaz (“singing, song”), from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ- (“to sing”). Cognate with Scots sang, song (“singing, song”), Saterland Frisian Song (“song”), West Frisian sang (“song”), Dutch zang (“song”), Low German sang (“song”), German Sang (“singing, song”), Swedish sång (“song”), Norwegian Bokmål sang (“song”), Norwegian Nynorsk song (“song”), Icelandic söngur (“song”), Ancient Greek ὀμφή (omphḗ, “voice, oracle”). More at sing.

senses.d: A musical composition with lyrics for voice or voices, performed by singing.
ex: Thomas listened to his favorite song on the radio yesterday.
The Harpe. […] A harper with his wreſt maye tune the harpe wrong / Mys tunying of an Inſtrument ſhal hurt a true ſonge

senses.d: Any musical composition.
Poetical composition; poetry; verse.
ex: This subject for heroic song.
The bard that first adorned our native tongue / Tuned to his British lyre this ancient song.

senses.d: The act or art of singing.
A melodious sound made by a bird, insect, whale or other animal.
ex: I love hearing the song of canary birds.
That most ethereal of all sounds, the song of crickets.

senses.d: The distinctive sound that a male bird utters to attract a mate or to protect his territory; contrasts with call; also, similar vocalisations made by female birds.
A low price, especially one under the expected value; chiefly in for a song.
ex: He bought that car for a song.
his [a common soldier's] pay is a song.

senses.d: An object of derision; a laughing stock.
ex: And now am I their song, yea, I am their byword.

grp.label: the act or art of singing
